First of all let me be honest, I have built a firearm from scratch. Just started with a nickle steel bar and Russian Olive wood. I was an armorer in the US Army and built match weapons, (.45 ACP's and M-14's) for the 6th US Army and 6th Army area National Guard and Army Reserve Units at the Presidio of San Francisco. I used a Bridgeport 9" X 42" vertical Milling machine that I bought off of Ebay for around 3 grand and a Bolton BT800 16" X 30" combination lathe and with a mill drilling head which cost me $1750.00. Of course the shipping charges were rather steep as these puppies are big and heavy. I used the BT800 to make the barrel and the Mill to make a Mauser type action. The rifle was a 8 X 61 mm. (30-06 blown out to .324 neck diameter.) The biggest problem was to get the proper heat treating of the components after machining. I used a Ceramic Kiln for my heat treating. Ceramic Kiln have really accurate temperature measurement sensors. The only thing I didn't make were the springs. (Wolf gun springs does a better Job a lot cheaper than I will) The most satisfying part was the making of the rifle stock out of Russian Olive.

So if you want to be a good gun smith first become a good machinist. (Plus with an investment of about $10,000 you are now set up to be able to bid on jobs from manufacturers that don't want to bother purchasing equipment and setting up for a small production run.) You can make a pretty good living doing that kind of thing. The ability to work wood also allows you to build custom furniture which there is a market for. Once you become a machinist you can make just about any thing. But REMEMBER a good fire arm is more a work of art than a simple tool.

Last but not least I have recently converted my equipment over to become a CNC equipment. I just chuck up metal stock, index the cutting heads and let it run.

TSJC and apprenticed. Colorado school of trades is also ok. Need tools, talent, and discipline. Wouldn't want to live in Pa, though there us a good school there. Broader education never hurts, but they teach enough basics at the good schools if you learn everything you can. Would be good to already know how to machine and weld and have a good knowledge of basic mechanics, wood working, and reloading. Then you can spend your time on gun specific stuff.
